# What Happens If You Don’t Register for PF or ESI? Consequences Every Indian Employer Must Know


October 12, 2026


[Shashank Yadav](https://salarybox.in/blog/author/shashank87cc9f270b/)


[No comments yet](https://salarybox.in/blog/what-happens-if-you-dont-register-for-pf-or-esi-consequences-every-indian-employer-must-know/#respond)


“We only have 22 employees. EPFO won’t notice us.”


“We deduct PF from salaries but haven’t deposited it yet. We will do it next quarter.”


“Our company has been running for 3 years without ESI registration. Nothing happened so far.”


These are the kinds of statements that have led Indian business owners to receive arrest warrants, property attachment orders, and penalty notices worth lakhs of rupees. In 2024, former Indian cricketer Robin Uthappa faced an arrest warrant over alleged misappropriation of ₹23.36 lakh in employee PF contributions from his company. In Faridabad, EPFO served notices to 696 defaulting establishments and recovered ₹6.16 crore from 70 units in a single enforcement drive.


The Employees’ Provident Fund Organisation (EPFO) is not a passive regulator. It has established a dedicated task force and an Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC) cell to recover over ₹26,700 crore in pending PF dues from defaulting employers across India. If you are an employer who has not registered for PF or ESI despite being required to, or worse, if you have been deducting contributions from employee salaries without depositing them, this guide explains exactly what you are facing.


## Who Must Register? A Quick Recap


Before diving into consequences, let us be clear about when registration becomes mandatory.


Law When Registration Is Mandatory Registration Deadline


EPF (Provident Fund) 20 or more employees on any day Within 1 month of crossing threshold


ESI (Employee State Insurance) 10+ employees (factory) or 20+ (non-factory) Within 15 days of becoming applicable


Once your establishment crosses these thresholds, registration is not optional. It is not something you can “get around to” when convenient. The clock starts ticking from the day you hit the employee count, and penalties accumulate from that same day if you fail to register.


For a complete breakdown of which laws apply at which employee count, see our guide on[employee thresholds for PF, ESI, Gratuity, and Bonus](https://salarybox.in/blog/) .


## Consequence 1: Financial Penalties That Compound Daily


The financial penalties for PF and ESI non-compliance are not one-time fines. They are compounding charges that grow larger with every passing month.


### PF Penalties Under the EPF Act, 1952


Violation Penalty Legal Section


Non-registration when applicable Up to ₹5,000 fine + 1 year imprisonment Section 14(1)


Non-payment or delayed payment of contributions 12% annual interest on the overdue amount Section 7Q


Damages for delayed payment 1% per month of the total arrears (post June 15, 2024) Section 14B, Para 32A


Making false statements to avoid registration Up to ₹5,000 fine + 1 year imprisonment Section 14(2)


Repeat offence (second or subsequent conviction) Up to ₹25,000 fine + up to 3 years imprisonment Section 14AA


Obstructing an EPFO inspector Up to ₹5,000 fine + 1 year imprisonment Section 14(2A)


### How Damages Under Section 14B Are Calculated


The damage rates under Para 32A of the EPF Scheme were revised on June 15, 2024. Here is how they work now versus the old rates:


**Before June 15, 2024 (Sliding Scale):**


Delay Period Damage Rate (Per Annum)


Up to 2 months 5%


2 to 4 months 10%


4 to 6 months 15%


Beyond 6 months 25%


**After June 15, 2024 (Flat Rate):**


Delay Period Damage Rate


Any duration 1% per month (equivalent to 12% per annum)


The maximum damages under Section 14B are capped at 100% of the total arrears. But here is what makes this dangerous: the 1% per month is calculated on the total outstanding amount (principal plus Section 7Q interest), and it compounds. A delay of 25 months or more means the damages alone can equal the original contribution amount.


### Real Calculation Example


Let us say you have 25 employees and should have been registered for PF since January 2024 but did not register until October 2026 (a delay of 33 months). Assuming average basic salary of ₹12,000 per employee:


Component Calculation Amount


Monthly PF contribution (employer + employee) 25 employees × ₹12,000 × 24% ₹72,000/month


Total arrears (33 months) ₹72,000 × 33 ₹23,76,000


Interest under Section 7Q (12% p.a., approx.) Approximately 35% of arrears for 33 months ₹8,31,600


Damages under Section 14B (1% per month × 33 months) 33% of (₹23,76,000 + ₹8,31,600) ₹10,58,508


**Total liability** **₹42,66,108**


That is over ₹42 lakh for a 25-employee company that simply did not register on time. And this does not include the cost of criminal prosecution.


### ESI Penalties Under the ESI Act, 1948


Violation Penalty Legal Section


Non-registration when applicable Up to ₹5,000 fine Section 85


Non-payment of contributions 12% annual interest on overdue amount Section 39(5)(a)


Deducting employee share but not depositing Up to ₹5,000 fine + up to 2 years imprisonment Section 85(a)


Repeat offence Enhanced penalties Section 85


Filing false returns Up to ₹5,000 fine + up to 6 months imprisonment Section 85(d)


### ESI Interest Accumulation


ESI contributions are due by the 15th of the following month. If you miss the deadline, interest at 12% per annum starts accumulating immediately. Unlike PF, there is no formal “damages” framework for ESI, but the interest charges alone can be substantial.


ESI Delay Scenario Interest Calculation


6 months delay on ₹50,000 contribution ₹50,000 × 12% × 6/12 = ₹3,000


1 year delay on ₹1,00,000 contribution ₹1,00,000 × 12% × 1 = ₹12,000


2 years delay on ₹2,00,000 contribution ₹2,00,000 × 12% × 2 = ₹48,000


3 years delay on ₹3,00,000 contribution ₹3,00,000 × 12% × 3 = ₹1,08,000


## Consequence 2: Criminal Prosecution and Imprisonment


This is where the consequences move from financial to personal. Non-compliance with PF and ESI is not just a civil matter. It is a criminal offence in India.


### When Criminal Prosecution Happens


Scenario Criminal Charge Maximum Punishment


Not registering for PF despite having 20+ employees Section 14(1) of EPF Act ₹5,000 fine + 1 year imprisonment


Deducting PF from employee salary but not depositing to EPFO Section 405/406 of Indian Penal Code (Criminal Breach of Trust) Up to 3 years imprisonment


Repeat PF offence (second conviction) Section 14AA of EPF Act ₹25,000 fine + up to 3 years imprisonment


Not paying ESI contributions Section 85 of ESI Act ₹5,000 fine + up to 2 years imprisonment


Filing false declarations to avoid PF/ESI Relevant sections of respective Acts Imprisonment + fine


### The Criminal Breach of Trust Angle


This is the most serious legal risk, and many employers do not even know about it. If you deduct PF contributions from your employees’ salaries (the employee’s 12% share) but do not deposit that money with EPFO, it constitutes criminal breach of trust under Sections 405 and 406 of the Indian Penal Code (now Section 316 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023).


The Karnataka High Court has specifically ruled that employers who deduct PF from salaries and fail to remit it to EPFO can be prosecuted for criminal breach of trust. This is a non-bailable offence in many jurisdictions and can lead to imprisonment of up to 3 years.


The key distinction is:


Situation Legal Treatment


Employer does not register for PF at all Administrative offence under EPF Act (Section 14)


Employer registers but delays deposit by a few days Interest and damages under Sections 7Q and 14B


Employer deducts employee share from salary but does not deposit Criminal breach of trust (IPC 405/406 or BNS 316)


The third scenario is treated most severely because the employer is essentially misappropriating money that belongs to the employees. Courts have consistently held that PF contributions deducted from salary are held in trust by the employer and must be deposited within the prescribed time.


### Real Cases That Made Headlines


**Robin Uthappa (2024):** Former Indian cricketer Robin Uthappa faced an arrest warrant from a Bengaluru court over alleged misappropriation of ₹23.36 lakh in employee PF contributions. The company where he was a director had deducted PF from employee salaries but did not deposit the amounts with EPFO.


**Faridabad Enforcement Drive (2025):** EPFO served notices to 696 defaulting establishments in Faridabad and Palwal districts. Recovery proceedings were initiated against 70 units, and ₹6.16 crore was recovered. Arrest warrants were issued against 29 firms whose directors refused to comply.


**Sahara India (2026):** EPFO launched ₹1,200 crore recovery action against Sahara India group entities for unpaid PF dues, using the IBC cell to initiate proceedings.


## Consequence 3: Property Attachment and Asset Recovery


EPFO has sweeping recovery powers that go far beyond fines. When an employer defaults on PF contributions, EPFO can use the following enforcement mechanisms:


### Recovery Methods Available to EPFO


Recovery Method How It Works Legal Basis


Attachment of bank accounts EPFO sends orders to banks to freeze and attach the employer’s accounts Section 8B of EPF Act


Attachment of movable property Vehicles, equipment, inventory can be seized Para 111 of EPF Scheme


Attachment of immovable property Land, buildings, offices can be attached and auctioned Section 8B, Para 111


Recovery through land revenue authorities EPFO can use the District Collector’s office to recover dues as land revenue arrears Section 8B


IBC proceedings EPFO can file claims as a creditor under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code EPFO IBC Cell


Travel restrictions Passport seizure or Look Out Circular for directors in extreme default cases In coordination with law enforcement


### EPFO’s Task Force and IBC Cell


In 2025, EPFO established a dedicated task force and IBC cell to tackle the ₹26,700 crore in outstanding PF dues across India. Of this amount, approximately ₹4,800 crore was identified as immediately recoverable, and the task force has been aggressively pursuing defaulting employers through a combination of property attachment, bank account freezing, and IBC petitions.


This means the days of “flying under the radar” are numbered. EPFO is actively using technology (Aadhaar-linked databases, bank account tracing, and inter-departmental data sharing) to identify non-compliant establishments.


## Consequence 4: Backdated Liability (The Retrospective Trap)


One of the most painful consequences of delayed registration is that the liability is always backdated to the date when the law first became applicable to your establishment. EPFO does not say “since you registered today, start paying from today.” They say “you should have registered 3 years ago, so pay everything from 3 years ago.”


### How Backdated Liability Works


Scenario What EPFO Will Do


You had 20 employees since April 2023 but registered in October 2026 You owe contributions from April 2023, plus interest and damages for 42 months


You registered in 2024 but missed some monthly filings You owe the missed contributions plus Section 7Q interest and Section 14B damages


You reduced staff to 15 after having 22, and stopped paying PF “Once covered, always covered.” You still owe contributions for all remaining employees


### The Assessment Process


When EPFO discovers a non-registered establishment (through employee complaints, cross-referencing with ESI data, income tax returns, or the Ministry of Corporate Affairs database), they initiate assessment proceedings under Section 7A of the EPF Act. The EPFO officer:


1. Issues a notice to the employer to appear and produce records
2. Examines the establishment’s books, payroll records, and bank statements
3. Determines the period of default and the number of employees
4. Assesses the total contributions that should have been paid
5. Issues an order for payment of arrears plus interest and damages
6. If the employer does not pay, initiates recovery proceedings (property attachment, prosecution)


The employer does have the right to appeal to the EPF Appellate Tribunal, but must deposit a portion of the assessed amount (typically 75%) before the appeal can be heard.


## Consequence 5: Employee Lawsuits and Labour Court Claims


Non-registration does not just create problems with regulators. It creates liability toward your own employees.


Employee Action Consequence for Employer


Employee files complaint with EPFO about non-coverage EPFO initiates suo motu investigation of the entire establishment


Employee takes employer to Labour Court for denied PF benefits Court can order payment of all PF dues plus compensation


Employee injured or falls ill and has no ESI coverage Employer must bear the entire medical cost plus potential damages


Former employee discovers PF was never deposited Criminal complaint under IPC/BNS for breach of trust


### The ESI Medical Cost Trap


This is one of the most underappreciated risks of not registering for ESI. When an eligible employee (earning up to ₹21,000/month) falls seriously ill or is injured at work and the establishment is not ESI registered:


The employer has no ESI coverage to fall back on. The entire medical expense becomes the employer’s direct responsibility. In cases of workplace injury, the employer may also face claims under the Workmen’s Compensation Act, which can result in payouts of several lakhs.


ESI coverage provides medical treatment, sickness benefit (70% of wages for up to 91 days), disablement benefit, maternity benefit, and dependent’s benefit in case of death. Without ESI registration, the employer has no access to any of these benefits for eligible employees, and must fund everything out of pocket if an incident occurs.


## Consequence 6: Impact on Business Operations


### Disqualification from Government Contracts and Tenders


Many government contracts and tenders in India require bidders to submit their PF and ESI registration certificates as part of the qualification documents. Without active registration and compliance certificates, your business is automatically disqualified from:


Opportunity Type PF/ESI Compliance Required?


Central government tenders (GeM portal) Yes, PF and ESI certificates mandatory


State government contracts Yes, in most states


PSU vendor empanelment Yes


Defence contracts Yes, strict compliance verification


Bank loan applications (for working capital) Often checked as part of due diligence


Investor due diligence (funding rounds) Always checked


### Impact on Funding and Acquisition


For startups seeking funding, PF and ESI non-compliance is a red flag that surfaces during legal due diligence. Investors and their lawyers will check your EPFO and ESI filings as part of their compliance review. Outstanding PF/ESI liabilities (including backdated contributions) directly reduce the enterprise value and can derail funding rounds.


For businesses being acquired, pending PF and ESI liabilities are treated as contingent liabilities that the buyer either deducts from the purchase price or requires the seller to settle before closing.


## Consequence 7: No Protection Under EPFO Vishwas Scheme Forever


The EPFO launched the Vishwas Scheme 2026 (announced at the 238th CBT meeting and implemented in 2026) as a one-time settlement window for employers with pending damages and penalty disputes. The scheme offers reduced damage rates:


Vishwas Scheme Category Reduced Damage Rate


Defaults up to 2 months 0.25% per month


Defaults up to 4 months 0.50% per month


Standard (all other defaults) 1% per month


This scheme is available for a limited window of 6 months. Once it expires, the standard damage rates apply, and future schemes are not guaranteed. Employers who continue to delay registration and compliance miss out on these amnesty opportunities.


## How Much Could You Actually Owe? Scenario Calculator


Here are three realistic scenarios showing the total liability an employer could face for non-compliance at different scales:


### Scenario 1: Small Shop in Delhi with 22 Employees (3 Years Default)


Parameter Details


Employees 22


Average basic salary ₹10,000/month


Default period 36 months (January 2024 to December 2026)


Liability Component Calculation Amount


PF arrears (24% of basic × 22 × 36) ₹2,400 × 22 × 36 ₹19,00,800


Section 7Q interest (12% p.a., approx.) ~40% of arrears for 3 year average ₹7,60,320


Section 14B damages (1% × 36 months on total) 36% of (₹19,00,800 + ₹7,60,320) ₹9,58,003


Penalty (if prosecuted) Fine up to ₹5,000


Legal and compliance costs Approximate ₹50,000 to ₹1,00,000


**Total potential liability** **₹37,24,123 to ₹37,74,123**


### Scenario 2: Manufacturing Unit in Gujarat with 50 Employees (2 Years PF and ESI Default)


Parameter Details


Employees 50 (30 earning below ₹21,000, 20 above)


Average basic salary ₹14,000/month


Default period 24 months


Liability Component Amount


PF arrears (24% × ₹14,000 × 50 × 24) ₹40,32,000


ESI arrears (4% × ₹18,000 average × 30 eligible × 24) ₹5,18,400


Section 7Q PF interest (12% p.a.) ₹9,67,680


ESI interest (12% p.a.) ₹1,24,416


Section 14B damages (1% × 24 months) ₹11,99,923


**Total potential liability** **₹68,42,419**


### Scenario 3: IT Company in Bengaluru with 35 Employees (Deducted PF but Never Deposited for 18 Months)


This is the most dangerous scenario because it involves criminal breach of trust.


Parameter Details


Employees 35


Average basic salary ₹20,000/month


Default period 18 months


PF was deducted from salaries Yes (employee share of 12% deducted but not deposited)


Liability Component Amount


PF arrears (employer 13% + employee 12% × ₹15,000 cap × 35 × 18) ₹23,62,500


Employee PF (deducted but not deposited, treated as misappropriation) ₹11,34,000


Section 7Q interest ₹4,25,250


Section 14B damages ₹5,03,775


**Total financial liability** **₹44,25,525**


**Criminal liability** Prosecution under IPC 405/406 (Criminal Breach of Trust), up to 3 years imprisonment


Note: In Scenario 3, the directors of the company can face personal criminal prosecution. This is not limited to the company as an entity. The individuals who made the decision to not deposit the deducted PF can be held personally liable.


## How to Fix Non-Compliance Before EPFO Finds You


If you are currently non-compliant, the best time to fix it was when you first became liable. The second best time is right now.


**Step 1: Determine your exact date of applicability**


Go through your employee records and find the first date on which you had 20 or more employees (for PF) or 10/20 (for ESI). All contributions must be paid from that date.


**Step 2: Register immediately**


Apply for PF registration on the EPFO Unified Portal (unifiedportal-emp.epfindia.gov.in) and for ESI registration on the ESIC portal (esic.gov.in). Registration typically takes 3 to 7 working days.


**Step 3: Calculate your total liability**


Work with a payroll professional or use[payroll software](https://salarybox.in/what-is-payroll-software-how-it-works-in-india-with-pf-esi-tds-2025-ultimate-guide/) to calculate the total arrears, interest, and damages owed. This needs to be accurate because incorrect calculations lead to further notices.


**Step 4: Check if the Vishwas Scheme is still open**


If the EPFO Vishwas 2026 scheme window is still active, apply under it for reduced damage rates. This can save you up to 50% to 75% on damages.


**Step 5: Make the payment and file all pending returns**


Deposit all arrears along with interest and damages. File all pending monthly ECR (Electronic Challan cum Return) for PF and half-yearly returns for ESI.


**Step 6: Set up automated compliance going forward**


Use[SalaryBox](https://salarybox.in/best-payroll-software-in-india-for-smes-and-startups-in-2025/) or similar[payroll management software](https://salarybox.in/blog/how-can-payroll-management-software-benefit-msmes-and-startups-in-india/) to automate PF and ESI calculations and ensure timely deposits every month. This eliminates the risk of future defaults.


**Step 7: Keep records for at least 5 years**


Maintain all payroll records, PF challans, ESI contribution receipts, and compliance certificates for at least 5 years. EPFO can audit records going back several years.

## How EPFO Catches Non-Compliant Employers


Many employers wonder how EPFO discovers unregistered establishments. Here are the primary detection methods:


Detection Method How It Works


Employee complaints Any employee can report non-coverage on the EPFO portal or through the helpline


Cross referencing with Income Tax data EPFO shares data with the Income Tax Department; salary payments visible in TDS returns reveal employee counts


Ministry of Corporate Affairs data Company incorporation records show director details, registered addresses, and authorized employee counts


GST registration data EPFO can access GST data to identify businesses that are operational and likely have employees


ESIC cross referencing If you are registered with ESI but not PF (or vice versa), the discrepancy triggers investigation


Labour Inspector visits State labour departments conduct regular inspections of factories and establishments


Bank transaction monitoring Large payroll transactions visible in bank records can trigger EPFO inquiry


Aadhaar and UAN database EPFO can identify employees whose UAN exists but shows no active contributions


## Why “We Are Too Small to Get Caught” Is a Dangerous Bet


Some business owners believe that EPFO only goes after large companies. This is factually incorrect. Here is why:


1. **EPFO’s enforcement is driven by employee complaints, not company size.** A single disgruntled employee filing a complaint on the EPFO portal can trigger a full investigation of your establishment.
2. **Digital data makes hiding impossible.** If you file TDS returns showing salary payments to 25 employees but have no PF registration, EPFO can flag the discrepancy automatically.
3. **The “once covered, always covered” rule means you cannot escape.** Even if you bring employees below 20, if you ever crossed the threshold, you remain covered permanently.
4. **State level enforcement is increasing.** Many state labour departments now conduct joint inspections covering PF, ESI, Shops and Establishments Act, and Minimum Wages Act in a single visit.
5. **Post Covid and post Code on Social Security, 2020, EPFO has modernized enforcement.** Digital tools, data analytics, and inter-departmental data sharing make detection faster than ever before.

## Frequently Asked Questions


### 1. What is the penalty for late deposit of PF contributions by even one day?


If you deposit PF contributions even one day after the 15th of the following month, you are liable for interest under Section 7Q at 12% per annum on the delayed amount. Additionally, damages under Section 14B apply at 1% per month of the arrears (post June 15, 2024 rate). For example, if your monthly PF contribution of ₹50,000 is deposited on the 20th instead of the 15th, you owe interest plus 1% damages for one month (₹500 in damages alone). While EPFO may not immediately prosecute for a few days’ delay, the interest and damages are automatically calculated and shown as outstanding in your EPFO account.


### 2. Can the directors of a company be personally prosecuted for PF/ESI defaults?


Yes. Under Section 14(1) of the EPF Act, “the employer” includes the manager, managing director, or any person responsible for the management and supervision of the establishment. Courts have held that directors who were in charge of the company’s affairs at the time of the default can be personally prosecuted. In the Robin Uthappa case, the arrest warrant was issued against him as a director of the defaulting company. Under the ESI Act as well, Section 86 holds the principal officer or director in charge personally liable.


### 3. Does EPFO send a notice before initiating prosecution?


EPFO typically follows a progression: first a reminder notice, then an assessment notice under Section 7A, then a demand notice for payment of arrears plus interest and damages, and finally prosecution under Section 14 if the employer does not comply. However, in cases of criminal breach of trust (deducting employee PF but not depositing), prosecution can be initiated more directly based on employee complaints. The employer has the right to respond at each stage, but ignoring notices significantly worsens the outcome.


### 4. What happens if I voluntarily register now after being non-compliant for 2 years?


Voluntary registration does not erase the past liability. EPFO will require you to pay all contributions from the date the law first became applicable (the date you had 20+ employees), plus interest under Section 7Q and damages under Section 14B. However, voluntary registration and proactive payment demonstrates good faith, which can work in your favour if damages are contested before the EPFO Appellate Tribunal. It is also possible that the Vishwas Scheme (if still open) can reduce your damage liability.


### 5. Can an employee file a police complaint if PF was deducted from salary but not deposited?


Yes. If an employer deducts the employee’s 12% PF contribution from salary but does not deposit it with EPFO, the employee can file a First Information Report (FIR) with the police under Section 405/406 of the IPC (Criminal Breach of Trust), now Section 316 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita. This is a cognizable offence, meaning the police can arrest the accused without a warrant. The employee can also simultaneously file a complaint with the EPFO Regional Commissioner for recovery of the unpaid contributions.


### 6. Is there any exemption for startups from PF/ESI registration?


No. There is no startup specific exemption from PF or ESI registration under current Indian law. Whether your company is a 2 year old startup or a 50 year old manufacturing unit, if you cross the 20 employee threshold for PF or the 10/20 employee threshold for ESI, registration is mandatory. Some startups choose to keep their employee count below 20 by using contractors or freelancers, but this approach has its own legal risks under the Contract Labour Act if the workers are essentially employees.


### 7. What is the difference between Section 7Q (interest) and Section 14B (damages)?


Section 7Q provides for simple compensatory interest at 12% per annum on the unpaid contributions. This is automatic and non-waivable; it applies regardless of the reason for delay. Section 14B provides for punitive damages, calculated at 1% per month (post June 15, 2024) on the total arrears. Damages under Section 14B are discretionary, and the employer can request a hearing before the EPFO officer to present reasons for the delay. Both charges are applied on top of the principal arrears, so the total liability includes original contribution plus Section 7Q interest plus Section 14B damages.


### 8. Can EPFO attach my personal property (not just the company’s property)?


For sole proprietorships and partnership firms, yes. The personal assets of the proprietor or partners can be attached for PF recovery because there is no legal distinction between the business and its owners. For private limited companies, EPFO typically attaches the company’s assets first. However, if the company is unable to pay and directors are found personally liable under Section 14, their personal assets can be pursued through separate legal proceedings. In cases involving criminal breach of trust, personal assets can be attached as part of the criminal proceedings.

*PF and ESI compliance is not something you can postpone or ignore. The consequences go beyond financial penalties and extend to criminal prosecution, property attachment, and loss of business opportunities.
